module-1: Press the Home button (round button at the bottom) once, or swipe up from the bottom edge on newer iPads, to return to your Home screen at any time — even if a scary pop-up has appeared.
You cannot break your iPad by tapping the wrong thing. Everything can be closed, undone, or fixed. Your device is designed to be forgiving.
To close a frozen app: double-press the Home button (or swipe up and pause on newer devices) to see open apps as cards, then swipe the frozen app's card upward off the screen.
module-2: Use the 3-Second Rule every time something feels off: Stop — Breathe — Verify. Pause before tapping any link or responding to any urgent message.
No real government agency (including the CRA) will ever demand payment by gift card, Bitcoin, or wire transfer. If someone asks this way, hang up immediately.
If you think you have been targeted by a scam, call the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre at 1-888-495-8501. Never feel embarrassed — reporting protects others too.
module-2.5: To send an Interac e-Transfer safely, verify the recipient's email address carefully before confirming — once accepted, it cannot be cancelled.
Take a screenshot of any confirmation page (press Side button + Volume Up at the same time on iPad/iPhone) to keep a record of bookings and transactions.

Turn on Automatic Updates so your apps and iPad software install improvements overnight while charging: Settings → App Store → App Updates, then Settings → General → Software Update → Automatic Updates.
module-3: Never use the same password for more than one account — if one is stolen, all accounts using that password become vulnerable.
Face ID and Touch ID are safe: your face or fingerprint data never leaves your device and is never sent to Apple or anyone else.
Use a passphrase (three or four random words strung together, such as 'purple-lamp-harbour-78') — it is both easier to remember and harder to crack than a short jumbled password.
module-4: Only ever download apps from the official App Store (Apple devices) or Google Play Store (Android). Never install an app from a link in a text or email.
Before downloading, check that the app has thousands of reviews and the developer name matches the company you expect — scammers create fake lookalike apps.
If you are unsure about an app permission (like access to your contacts or camera), choose Don't Allow. You can always change this later in Settings, and saying no will not break the app.
module-5: Never tap a link in an email asking you to verify your account or confirm your identity. Legitimate companies will never ask for this by email — go directly to the website by typing the address yourself.
Check the sender's full email address (not just the display name) — scammers use addresses that look almost right, such as 'support@rbc-secure-alerts.com' instead of rbc.com.
Scam text messages claiming to be from Canada Post, your bank, or a delivery service are very common — delete any text with a suspicious link without tapping it.
module-6: Your bank will never phone, email, or text you to ask for your password, PIN, or security questions. If someone contacts you asking for these, hang up and call your bank directly using the number on the back of your card.
When shopping online, check that the web address starts with https:// (the 's' means secure) and look for the padlock icon before entering any payment details.
Always sign out fully when you finish online banking — especially on a shared computer. Simply closing the browser window is not enough.
module-7: Turn on iCloud Photos (Settings → your name → iCloud → Photos) to back up your photos automatically — they will be safe even if your iPad is lost, stolen, or damaged.
Deleting a photo does not remove it permanently straight away — it moves to Recently Deleted and stays there for 30 days, giving you plenty of time to change your mind.
You can share a photo album with specific family members without giving anyone access to your entire photo library — use the Shared Albums feature in the Photos app.
module-8: FaceTime is free and already installed on your iPhone and iPad — just open it and tap someone from your contacts to start a video call.
Prop your iPad up at eye level (a cookbook stand or a stack of books works well) and sit facing a window so the light falls on your face — this makes video calls much clearer.
Only add people you know and trust to group messages and shared photo albums. If you receive a group invitation from someone you do not recognise, do not join it.
module-9: AI tools like ChatGPT or Siri are very helpful but can make mistakes — always double-check important information (medical, legal, financial) from a trusted source such as your doctor or a reputable website.
Never share personal information with an AI chat tool: no Social Insurance Number, banking details, passwords, home address, or medical information. Your conversations may be saved.

If you receive a call or video that seems to be from a family member asking for money urgently, hang up and call that person back on their regular number — AI can now convincingly clone voices and faces.
module-10: Apps like PC Express (Loblaws/No Frills), Instacart, and Uber Eats let you order groceries or meals for delivery or curbside pickup — you always see the full cost before confirming.
Review your order carefully before tapping Place Order — check quantities, substitution preferences, and the delivery address.
Your payment information is protected with the same bank-level encryption used by major Canadian retailers — it is as safe as online shopping at any trusted Canadian store.
module-11: Before getting into any vehicle, do three checks: confirm the driver's name matches the app, confirm the licence plate matches, and confirm the driver says your first name without you prompting them.
If anything does not match — the plate is wrong, the driver seems unsure of your name, or something feels off — do NOT get in. Cancel the trip and request a new one. Your safety comes first.
Uber and Lyft confirm the price before you book — there are no surprise fares. You can also share your live trip details with a family member directly from inside the app.
module-12: When stuck in an automated phone system, say 'representative' or 'agent' clearly, or press 0 — this usually connects you to a real person faster.

Never allow remote access to your device if someone called YOU unexpectedly — even if the caller ID shows Apple, Microsoft, or your bank. Caller ID can be faked. Hang up and call the company back yourself.
Free help is available: Connected Canadians 1-855-808-0505 and Cyber-Seniors 1-844-217-3057 both offer patient, friendly tech support at no cost to you.
module-13: Set your Facebook privacy to Friends Only so strangers cannot see your posts: tap the three-line menu → Settings → Privacy → Who can see your future posts? → Friends.

Never send money to someone you have met only online, no matter how convincing their story. Romance scams cost Canadians over $50 million every year — there is no shame in being targeted, but the rule is firm.
If anyone on Facebook Marketplace or Instagram asks you to pay using gift cards, stop immediately. No legitimate seller ever accepts gift cards — it is always a scam.
module-14: Smart plugs are the safest and easiest place to start with smart home devices — they cost $15–$30, plug into any outlet, and let you control any lamp or appliance by voice or app.
Use a strong Wi-Fi password (at least 12 characters, not your address or birthday) to protect all smart home devices. Ask your internet provider to help if you are unsure.
You can press the physical mute button on any voice assistant (Alexa, Google Home) to stop it from listening at any time — a red light confirms the microphone is off.
module-15: Most telehealth video or phone appointments with your Ontario family doctor are covered by OHIP at no cost — just like an in-person visit. Ask your clinic if virtual appointments are available.
Ontario's free 24/7 nurse advice line is 1-866-797-0000. Call any time — evenings, weekends, or holidays — to speak with a registered nurse about your symptoms.
For your video appointment, sit in a quiet, well-lit room facing a window, test your camera and microphone a few minutes early, and have your health card and a list of your current medications ready.
module-16: Back up your photos and important documents to iCloud before travelling — if your device is lost or stolen, everything is recoverable when you get home.
Avoid using public Wi-Fi at airports, hotels, and coffee shops for banking or personal accounts. Use your phone's cellular data or a VPN instead.
Keep a printed copy of your passport photo page, travel insurance policy number, and emergency contact numbers in a separate bag from your main luggage.
module-17: AI tools can answer questions and help you write — but they sometimes state wrong information confidently. Always verify important facts with a second source.
Never share your Social Insurance Number, banking details, passwords, or home address with any AI chat tool. Your conversations may be stored.
A good prompt habit: tell the AI who you are and what you need — 'I am a Canadian senior looking for simple instructions on how to...' gets you clearer, more relevant answers.
module-18: Video calls with family do not require technical skill — just tap the FaceTime icon, tap someone in your contacts, and wait for them to answer. You can hang up at any time by pressing the red button.
Friendly Voices (1-855-892-5446) is a free Canadian service that matches seniors with a friendly volunteer for regular phone conversations.
Ask your local library what digital programmes they offer — many Ontario libraries run free Zoom clubs, tech help sessions, and interest-based online groups.
module-19: Make a list of your important online accounts (email, banking, social media) and store the list securely — in a sealed envelope with your will, or in a trusted password manager. This is a gift to your family.
You can set up a Legacy Contact on Facebook (Settings → General → Memorialisation Settings) to let a trusted person manage your account after you pass away.
Your photos stored in iCloud or on a hard drive are part of your digital estate. Decide now who you want to receive them, and include instructions in your will or estate planning documents.
module-visual-ai: Point your camera at any plant, bird, product label, or sign and tap the search icon (Visual Look Up on iPhone/iPad) to identify what you are looking at instantly — no typing required.
To scan a QR code, open your Camera app and point it at the code — a notification appears at the top with the link. You do not need a separate QR scanner app.

If you receive a suspicious letter or printed message and want help understanding it, take a clear photo and send it to a family member via text — you get a second opinion without handing over the original.
